text: Heinrich Vogl (15 January 1845 – 21 April 1900) was a German operatic heldentenor. He played the role of Loge in Richard Wagner's Das Rheingold at the Munich Court Opera on 22 September 1869, with his wife, Therese Vogl, performing as Wellgunde. He also sang the role of Siegmund in Wagner's Die Walküre at Munich on 26 June 1870, with Therese Vogl portraying Sieglinde, Siegmund's sister and lover. His debut at the Munich Court Opera was as Max in Weber's Der Freischütz. He performed at Bayreuth, Berlin, London, and the Metropolitan Opera in New York City. At Bayreuth, he played Loge in the first complete Ring cycle on 13 August 1876. His performance in the role earned fellow singer Lilli Lehmann's praise, who stated he was born for the part and that his Loge had never been equalled. His debut at the Metropolitan Opera was on 1 January 1890 in the title role of Lohengrin; he also performed Loge, Siegmund, the title role of Tannhäuser, Tristan in Tristan und Isolde, and Siegfried in both Siegfried and Götterdämmerung. Heinrich Vogl was the first to perform the roles of Loge and Siegfried in London, doing so in the first Ring cycle at Her Majesty's Theatre with Anton Seidl conducting and his wife playing Brünnhilde. His Wagner repertoire included all the leading tenor roles except Walther in Die Meistersinger von Nürnberg, for which Wagner rejected him for the 1868 premiere, stating at the age of 23 that Vogl was "totally incompetent." He and his wife Therese were among the first to sing the lead roles in Tristan und Isolde and were highly regarded in those roles. His non-Wagner roles included the title role in Verdi's Otello, Canio in Leoncavallo's Pagliacci, Aeneas in Berlioz's Les Troyens, and the title role of Berlioz's Benvenuto Cellini. He was known for his vocal power and stamina, enabling him to perform Loge, Siegmund, and both Siegfrieds from Wagner's Ring cycle on consecutive evenings multiple times. Heinrich Vogl is buried beside his wife in Tutzing, Bavaria.
